ai-at-work.title: NEA’s Tiffany Luck says enterprises are still figuring out their AI ROI
ai-at-work.excerpt: Tokenmaxxing was the hottest trend in Silicon Valley earlier this year, with CEOs encouraging employees to push AI usage as far as it would go. Then the bill came due. Uber reportedly blew through its
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Enterprises spent money on AI tools without measuring results, then got shocked when the bills arrived and nobody could prove the investment was working. This matters because digital workplace leaders are under pressure to justify every software dollar while executives still treat AI like a shiny toy, creating a credibility gap that's going to haunt procurement conversations for years. The real story here is that tokenmaxxing is just the latest example of tech solving for activity instead of outcomes, which is exactly how you end up with expensive Slack instances nobody actually uses.

ai-at-work.title: World leaders want American AI. They just don’t want America to be able to turn it off.
ai-at-work.excerpt: French President Macron and Indian PM Modi raised alarms at the G7 summit that the U.S. could cut off access to American AI overnight — a fear the Anthropic blackout just made real.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: World leaders are worried the U.S. could suddenly cut off access to American AI systems, and the recent Anthropic outage proved this isn't paranoia. For digital workplace pros, this matters because your organization's AI tools, workflows, and maybe your entire productivity stack could vanish if geopolitical tensions spike or regulations shift. Here's the reality: betting your workplace operations on American AI without a backup plan is like building your office in a rented building with no lease, which is exactly what half the Fortune 500 just did anyway.

ai-at-work.title: Anthropic becomes first AI startup to join the Frontier carbon removal coalition
ai-at-work.excerpt: Anthropic has joined the Frontier coalition, which received another $915M in pledges to fund carbon removal projects.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic, the AI startup behind Claude, joined Frontier, a coalition that funds carbon removal technology, bringing the coalition's pledges to $915 million. This matters because digital workplace leaders are increasingly expected to understand their organization's AI carbon footprint and sustainability commitments, making this a signal worth watching. Still, it's worth noting that pledging money to carbon removal is easier than actually reducing emissions in the first place, but at least someone's thinking about the problem while the rest of us argue about whether Slack uses too much bandwidth.

ai-at-work.title: Social media’s next evolution: user-controlled algorithms
ai-at-work.excerpt: Social media feeds are becoming more customizable as platforms like Threads, Instagram, and TikTok introduce tools that let users directly influence the algorithms powering their recommendations.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Meta platforms are finally letting users tweak their own algorithmic feeds instead of just accepting whatever the black box decides to show them. This matters because digital workplace pros have spent years trying to get employees to engage with internal social tools that feel like the algorithmic wild west, so user control could actually make people want to use these platforms instead of treating them like corporate punishment. About time someone asked users what they wanted instead of just optimizing for engagement metrics and wondering why people are mad all the time.

tools-tech.title: Does your phone charge as fast as advertised? I measured the latest iPhone, Samsung, OnePlus
tools-tech.excerpt: Phone makers love to advertise fast-charging speeds. I tested three flagship phones with OEM and Anker chargers to see what their claims really mean.
tools-tech.dwp_take: A tech reviewer put flagship phones from Apple, Samsung, and OnePlus through real-world charging tests and found the actual speeds don't match the marketing promises. This matters to digital workplace folks because half your workforce is probably running their entire work life off a phone battery, and if your team is burning through juice before lunch, productivity takes a hit. Here's the truth: phone makers have been gaming the charging speed conversation for years, and honestly, it's time they just told us how long it actually takes to go from dead to usable instead of throwing around megawatts like they're comparing shoe sizes.

tools-tech.title: How companies are racing to solve the AI token problem
tools-tech.excerpt: Because generative AI (genAI) tools and services have become so ubiquitous (and popular), the costs of using them are going through the roof — leading to an insatiable appetite for tokens. Tokens repr
tools-tech.dwp_take: Companies are scrambling to manage exploding AI costs as token consumption skyrockets across their organizations. This matters because digital workplace leaders now have to make real decisions about which AI tools get budget priority, how to govern AI spending, and whether employees are using these tools efficiently or just chatting with chatbots for fun. It's basically the cloud cost management problem all over again, except this time everyone's panicking because they greenlit AI everywhere without thinking about what it would actually cost.

tools-tech.title: Judge signals AI recruitment tool vendors like Workday may not escape liability for discrimination
tools-tech.excerpt: A federal judge has rebuffed Workday’s claim that it cannot be held liable under California anti-discrimination laws when its tools are used to screen (and potentially reject) job candidates in other
tools-tech.dwp_take: A federal judge is saying Workday can't hide behind state boundaries to dodge discrimination liability when its AI recruitment tools screen out job candidates. This matters because vendors have been banking on legal gray areas to avoid responsibility for biased algorithms, but this ruling suggests they're now on the hook regardless of where their clients operate. After thirty years watching tech companies promise they'll "self-regulate," I'm genuinely shocked a judge is actually making them sweat a little.

tools-tech.title: Anthropic Fable dispute suggests ‘export’ no longer means what it used to
tools-tech.excerpt: For generations, technology export controls referred to the transfer of source code to other countries. But that no longer works, as the latest Anthropic fight with the US Commerce Department makes cl
tools-tech.dwp_take: Anthropic got told by the US Commerce Department to block foreign nationals from accessing its AI models, regardless of where they are, which fundamentally changes what "export controls" actually mean in the AI era. This matters because it signals that regulators now view access to running AI systems the same way they view physical technology transfers, which has massive implications for how global teams can collaborate on digital workplace tools. After thirty years watching tech policy, I can tell you that when bureaucrats stop caring about whether code leaves the building and start caring about who can use it while in the building, everybody's compliance spreadsheets just got a lot longer and messier.

digital-culture.title: The competitive advantage AI can’t automate
digital-culture.excerpt: Anthropic recently posted a job opening for a Head of GTM Narrative. Not a content lead. Not a brand director. A go-to-market narrative strategist. The company that has spent years building some of th
digital-culture.dwp_take: Anthropic hired a Head of GTM Narrative role, betting that storytelling and strategic messaging are the competitive advantage that AI can't replicate. This matters because it signals to digital workplace leaders that while automation handles repetitive work, human narrative strategy and authentic communication are becoming more valuable, not less. After thirty years watching technology trends, I can tell you the irony is delicious: the AI company figured out that what separates winners from losers is still the thing that's hardest to code.

digital-culture.title: Workers are judging companies for their silence on LGBTQ+ issues
digital-culture.excerpt: The sustained attacks on diversity, equity, and inclusion programs have left corporate America hesitant to speak out forcefully on LGBTQ+ issues—and that silence has not gone unnoticed. Companies that
digital-culture.dwp_take: Companies are pulling back from public LGBTQ+ advocacy and dropping out of inclusion rankings, mostly because the political environment got hostile toward DEI initiatives. This matters because your workforce is watching, and silence reads as a choice to digital natives who expect their employers to stand for something beyond quarterly earnings. Here's the thing: you can't build trust by standing nowhere, and employees remember which companies went quiet when it got uncomfortable.

digital-culture.title: The Korean Telecom Giant at the Center of Anthropic’s Mythos Controversy
digital-culture.excerpt: Days before Anthropic took its most advanced AI models offline, the White House ordered the company to revoke SK Telecom’s access to Claude Mythos over claims of alleged ties to China.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Anthropic pulled Claude Mythos offline and revoked SK Telecom's access after White House pressure over alleged Chinese connections. This matters to digital workplace pros because it shows how geopolitical tensions are now directly interfering with which enterprise AI tools you can actually use, adding another layer of compliance complexity on top of everything else you're already managing. The irony is delicious: we spent years worried about AI vendors locking us in, and now governments are doing it for us.

digital-culture.title: Operating a Humanoid With Your Body Is a Hot Job in China’s Hardware Capital
digital-culture.excerpt: In Shenzhen, workers at IO-AI Tech control humanoid robots using a VR rig reminiscent of Ready Player One.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Workers in Shenzhen are remotely operating humanoid robots through VR rigs, essentially becoming the robot's nervous system from a distance. This matters because it's the most literal interpretation yet of "hybrid work" and raises real questions about job design, worker fatigue, and what we're actually building these tools for in the digital workplace. Look, if we're going to spend billions on automation, the irony of creating exhausting new jobs that require someone to strap on a VR headset and become a robot all day is pretty rich.

industry-news.title: IBM Report: Most EMEA Executives Don’t Fully Understand Their AI Dependencies
industry-news.excerpt: IBM research finds many EMEA executives lack visibility into AI dependencies, raising risks around cost, outages, vendor lock-in, and sovereignty. The post IBM Report: Most EMEA Executives Don’t Fully
industry-news.dwp_take: A new IBM report shows that most European, Middle Eastern, and African executives can't actually see where their AI systems depend on specific vendors or technologies, which creates real risks around costs, service failures, and data sovereignty. This matters because digital workplace leaders are increasingly building AI into their operations without understanding the underlying infrastructure, which means they could get blindsided by outages, unexpected bills, or regulatory problems. Here's the thing: after thirty years in this space, I've seen this movie before with cloud migration, and it never ends well when leadership doesn't know what they actually own.

industry-news.title: Modernizing Meeting Spaces: How Agentic Control and Intelligent Framing Redefine Hybrid Work
industry-news.excerpt: Neat is using agentic AI, intelligent framing, and flexible room modes to turn passive video endpoints into “thinking spaces,” giving IT a blueprint to modernize meeting rooms for hybrid work. The pos
industry-news.dwp_take: Neat is pushing AI-powered meeting room technology that automatically adjusts cameras, lighting, and room settings based on who's participating and how they're working together. For IT leaders managing hybrid spaces, this matters because it promises to eliminate the painful reality of people hunched over laptops while sitting in rooms with perfectly good cameras nobody knows how to use. Look, if we need AI to figure out which direction the camera should point, we've probably overcomplicated the whole thing, but I'll take functional over fancy any day.

industry-news.title: 105K Chrome Installs Linked to Adware and Fake Google Traffic
industry-news.excerpt: Socket researchers linked 152 Chrome wallpaper extensions to hidden data logging, fake Google search traffic, and ad monetization. The post 105K Chrome Installs Linked to Adware and Fake Google Traffi
industry-news.dwp_take: Socket researchers discovered that 152 Chrome wallpaper extensions with over 105,000 combined installs were secretly logging user data, generating fake Google search traffic, and monetizing ads without user knowledge. This matters because your workforce is installing these things thinking they're harmless customization tools while actually giving bad actors access to browsing habits and search patterns. Here's the thing: we spend all this time implementing security policies and then someone installs a pretty sunset wallpaper and torches the whole operation.

industry-news.title: Apple to Merge Private Mail Domains for Sign In and Hide My Email
industry-news.excerpt: Apple will move new Sign in with Apple and Hide My Email relay addresses to private.icloud.com, requiring developer updates. The post Apple to Merge Private Mail Domains for Sign In and Hide My Email
industry-news.dwp_take: Apple is consolidating its email relay services under the private.icloud.com domain, which means developers need to update their authentication integrations to keep things working smoothly. For digital workplace pros managing SSO systems and identity infrastructure, this matters because poorly planned migrations can create authentication headaches across your entire user base if you're not on top of it. Here's the thing though: Apple keeps making these backend shifts without enough warning, and someone in your org is going to miss the deadline and suddenly wonder why login is broken at 4 PM on a Friday.
